newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens hi-tech sales rising overseas.
newsitem.headline: Siemens hi-tech sales rising overseas.

text.p: German industrial group Siemens AG, although expecting flat profit this year, is having little trouble leveraging foreign markets to boost sales in its computer and communications businesses.

Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG (SNI) said on Thursday at the CeBIT trade fair that a rebound in Europe outside of Germany led worldwide sales to rise 13 percent to 5.7 billion marks ($3.32 billion) in the first five months of business year 1996/97.

In the same period, sales in communications -- which includes the public and private telecommunications units and a defence electronics business -- climbed 18 percent to 9.5 billion marks in the first five months of business year 1996/97.

"There is hardly a company anywhere like Siemens with a full telecommunications portfolio and the products of Siemens Nixdorf," said management board member Volker Jung at CeBIT. "This makes us a system integrator for communications, capable of providing worldwide solutions from a single source."

Siemens was less forthcoming on its profits. Jung said communications profit would rise at the same rate as sales. The three last year generated pretax profit of 832 million marks -- more than a quarter of the group total.
SNI chief Gerhard Schulmeyer gave no earnings outlook. In 1995/96, pretax profit was 52 million marks and net income 29 million marks as sales rose seven percent to 13.9 billion marks.
In November Siemens warned 1996/97 profit would not improve over last year, in large part because falling computer memory chip prices were eroding profit in its semiconductor unit.
SNI was lifted in the first five months of 1996/97 by sales gains of 36 percent in Italy, 25 percent in Austria and 19 percent in France, said unit chief Gerhard Schulmeyer.
In Germany, SNI sales rose 11 percent to 3.5 billion marks. Internationally, sales climbed 21 percent to 2.2 billion marks.
"Germany is investing in computer technology at half the rate fo the United States, and even France and Great Britain are ahead of us," Schulmeyer said.
SNI figures take into account the loss of revenue from the sale of a 900 million-mark high-end printer business last year.

Public networks (ON), which sells switches, cables and othergear to phone companies, saw sales in the five-month period 30 rise 26 percent to five billion marks whileorders increased 26 percent to 7.4 billion marks.
Private networks (PN), which makes cordless, cellular and standard telephone sets, saw sales in the period climb 15 percent to four billion marks and orders 14 percent to 4.2 billion marks.
Jung said PN is the world's top supplier of telephone sets,while ON equipment routed one tenth of all calls worldwide.
He gave no figures for the defense electronics business, forwhich Siemens was seeking a buyer or joint venture partner. ($1=1.7153 Mark)
